claims.text: A hybrid CALPHAD–MLIP framework can accurately predict melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity for refractory high-entropy alloys.
CALPHAD can provide a thermodynamically consistent baseline for multicomponent phase stability.
CALPHAD can estimate initial melting points for the proposed RHEA screening workflow.
High-throughput CALPHAD can automatically perform thousands of calculations and screen compositions using user-defined criteria.
Moment Tensor Potentials can be trained on DFT data spanning elemental, binary, ternary, and multicomponent configurations.
For MoNbTaW, an MTP can reproduce DFT energies and forces with low errors while balancing accuracy and computational cost.
MLIP molecular dynamics using two-phase coexistence or free-energy methods can compute melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity for RHEAs.
Chemical short-range order and local lattice distortions modulate phonon spectra and anharmonic vibrational contributions to RHEA thermodynamic properties.
MLIPs capture SRO-dependent local-environment effects relevant to material behavior.
MLIPs capture SRO-induced variations in vibrational entropy and anharmonicity.
Standard EAM or MEAM empirical potentials fail to capture the multi-body interactions and SRO needed for accurate melting-property predictions.
Pure DFT is computationally prohibitive for screening vast multicomponent compositional spaces.
CALPHAD screening reduces the search space required for MLIP training and validation.
The example RHEAs have melting points above 2000 K and sparse experimental thermodynamic data.
The hybrid framework will predict RHEA melting temperatures within ±50 K.
The hybrid framework will have a computational cost orders of magnitude lower than pure DFT.
The hybrid framework will predict melting properties more accurately than empirical potentials.
The methodology is valid for single-phase BCC or FCC solid solutions in which SRO is the dominant microstructural feature.
Systems with complex intermetallic precipitation or phase separation require explicit phase-field modeling and fall outside the method's validity.
Conventional CALPHAD implementations have low efficiency when exploring an entire multicomponent composition–temperature space.
